guide.summary: Pacific art spans Micronesia, Melanesia, and Polynesia. Many works express mana (spiritual power), genealogy, and social status, and are activated through ceremony, exchange, and performance. Materials are often perishable (feathers, bark cloth, wood), and some works were made to be destroyed or given away. Colonial encounters reshaped both art and its collection.

sections.heading: Monuments and navigation
sections.body:
**Nan Madol** (Pohnpei, Micronesia) is a complex of artificial islets built from basalt columns stacked log-cabin style, a ceremonial and political center of the Saudeleur dynasty.

On Rapa Nui (Easter Island), **moai on platforms (ahu)** represent deified ancestors. They face inland, toward the communities they protect, rather than out to sea.

The **Navigation chart** of the Marshall Islands, made of sticks and shells, models ocean swells and islands. Navigators memorized such charts on land rather than carrying them at sea, showing art as knowledge.

sections.heading: Power, status, and the divine
sections.body:
Hawaiian **'ahu 'ula** (feather capes) were made from thousands of red and yellow feathers attached to a fiber net. They signified chiefly rank and mana; Captain Cook received some as gifts, and many entered European collections.

The **Staff god** of Rarotonga (Cook Islands) was wrapped in layers of bark cloth that concealed a carved wooden core; missionaries removed and destroyed many wrappings. The **Female deity from Nukuoro** (Micronesia) is a smooth, abstract wooden figure, prized later by European modernists.

**Tamati Waka Nene** (1890), an oil portrait by the European painter Gottfried Lindauer, shows a Māori chief with facial tattoo (moko) and cloak, made after the subject's death from a photograph, reflecting both Māori status and colonial portraiture.

sections.heading: Ceremony, exchange, and impermanence
sections.body:
**Malagan** displays of New Ireland (Papua New Guinea) honor the dead in elaborate carved and painted ceremonies; afterward, objects are often destroyed, discarded, or sold, since their purpose is fulfilled.

The Torres Strait **Buk** mask, made of turtle shell, was used in funerary and initiation ceremonies.

Bark cloth (**tapa**, or hiapo in Niue) was made by women, beaten from mulberry bark and decorated, and used in exchange and ceremony.

The **Presentation of Fijian mats and tapa cloths to Queen Elizabeth II** (1953) was a performance of exchange during the queen's visit: textiles presented with ceremony conveyed relationship and obligation, not simply gifts.

keyTakeaways: Pacific art often embodies mana, genealogy, and rank.
Many works are activated through ceremony, performance, and exchange.
Perishable materials and planned destruction (malagan) challenge museum ideas of permanence.
Women's arts like tapa carry high social value.
Navigation charts show art as a technology of knowledge.
Colonial encounters affected materials, subjects, and where works ended up.
commonMistakes: Saying the moai face the sea.
Assuming navigators carried stick charts during voyages.
Treating malagan objects as permanent artworks.
Ignoring women as makers of high-status objects like tapa.
Describing the 1953 presentation as merely a gift rather than a ceremonial exchange.
examTips: Use "mana" and genealogy in explanations of status objects.
Contextual analysis works well with malagan, staff gods, and feather capes.
Performance and exchange are central: describe how works were used.
Note perishable materials and their implications for survival and display.
Colonial encounters provide strong evidence for continuity-and-change prompts.
guide.cramSheet:
**Micronesia:** Nan Madol (basalt) · Nukuoro female deity · Marshall Islands navigation chart

**Polynesia:** moai on ahu (face inland) · 'ahu 'ula feather cape (Hawai'i, mana) · Rarotonga staff god (bark cloth, missionaries) · hiapo (Niue) · Tamati Waka Nene (Lindauer, moko) · Fijian mats/tapa to Elizabeth II (1953)

**Melanesia:** malagan (New Ireland, ephemeral) · Buk mask (Torres Strait, turtle shell)

vocab.definition: Spiritual power or prestige in Polynesian cultures, often associated with chiefs and sacred objects.
Monolithic ancestral figures on Rapa Nui (Easter Island).
A Hawaiian feather cape worn by high-ranking men.
Bark cloth made by beating the inner bark of trees, usually by women.
Bark cloth from Niue, often with fine freehand designs.
New Ireland funerary ceremonies and the carvings made for them.
Māori facial tattooing indicating identity and status.
A Marshall Islands navigation model of ocean swells and islands.
Volcanic rock, used in columnar form at Nan Madol.
Art intended to last only briefly or be destroyed after use.
Ceremonial giving that creates relationships and obligations.

practice.stimulus: Massive stone figures with elongated heads stand on stone platforms on Rapa Nui. Most face inland, toward villages.
practice.stem: The figures' orientation most likely reflects their role as

choices.text: deified ancestors watching over and protecting their communities
lighthouses guiding ships
decorations for European visitors
boundary markers facing rival islands

practice.explanation: Moai on ahu face their descendants' settlements, concentrating ancestral mana there.

distractors.B: They face away from the sea.

practice.stimulus: A semicircular cape is made from thousands of red and yellow bird feathers attached to a net of plant fiber. It was worn by high-ranking men.

choices.text: the wearer's chiefly rank and mana
membership in a missionary church
everyday protection from rain
a fisherman's trade

practice.explanation: 'Ahu 'ula required immense labor and rare feathers, marking sacred status.

practice.stimulus: A lattice of sticks lashed together, with small shells attached at intersections, represents patterns of ocean swells and the locations of islands.

choices.text: Navigators studied and memorized it on land to understand how swells bend around islands.
Sailors held it at sea like a printed map.
It was worn as a mask in ceremonies.
It was a decorative wall hanging for tourists.

practice.explanation: The navigation chart was a teaching tool; navigators relied on memory and the feel of the swells at sea.

distractors.B: Charts were usually left on shore.

practice.stem: In many Pacific cultures, bark cloth (tapa) was

choices.text: made by women and highly valued in ceremonial exchange
imported from China
made only by European missionaries
used only for everyday clothing with no status

practice.explanation: Women beat and decorated bark into cloth that carried wealth and social meaning.

practice.stimulus: Elaborate carved and painted wooden figures and masks are made for funerary ceremonies honoring the dead in New Ireland. After the ceremonies, the objects are often destroyed, left to decay, or sold.
practice.stem: This practice suggests that the objects' value lies primarily in

choices.text: their role in the ceremony, after which their purpose is complete
their permanence as museum pieces
their resale value to collectors
their use as everyday furniture

practice.explanation: Malagan carvings fulfill their function in commemoration; preserving them isn't the goal.

distractors.C: Some were sold, but that came after their ritual purpose.

practice.stimulus: A carved wooden staff from Rarotonga was once wrapped in layers of bark cloth that concealed its core. Many such wrappings were stripped and destroyed by missionaries in the 1800s, and some carved cores were sent to Europe.
practice.stem: Which statement best interprets the staff's history?

choices.text: Missionaries' removal of wrappings eliminated what made the staff sacred, reflecting the impact of conversion on Indigenous religious art.
The wrappings were added by museums for protection.
The staff was made for missionaries as a souvenir.
The staff was used to navigate canoes.

practice.explanation: The staff god's concealed, wrapped form held its sacred power; stripping it was an act of religious suppression.

distractors.B: The wrappings were original and integral.

practice.stimulus: On Pohnpei, a complex of nearly 100 artificial islets was built from stacked basalt columns, laid in alternating directions like logs, in shallow water near the coast.
practice.stem: The complex is best understood as

choices.text: a ceremonial and political center for a ruling dynasty
a European colonial fort
a temporary fishing camp
a Buddhist monastery

practice.explanation: Nan Madol served the Saudeleur rulers, with residential, mortuary, and ritual areas.

practice.stimulus: An 1890 oil portrait by a European-born painter living in New Zealand shows a Māori chief with full facial tattoo, wearing a cloak and holding a carved weapon. It was painted from a photograph after the chief's death.

choices.text: the meeting of Māori markers of status with European portrait conventions in a colonial context
a traditional Māori carving technique
an abstract modernist experiment
a Buddhist devotional image

practice.explanation: Lindauer's Tamati Waka Nene records moko and regalia in Western oil portraiture; such portraits could be valued by Māori as ancestral images.

distractors.B: It's an oil painting by a European artist.

practice.stimulus: During Queen Elizabeth II's 1953 visit to Fiji, women carried long rolls of mats and decorated bark cloth in procession and presented them to her, accompanied by speeches and ritual.
practice.stem: The event is best understood as

choices.text: a ceremonial performance of exchange that established relationships and obligations
a sale of textiles to the British government
a protest against colonial rule
a fashion show

practice.explanation: The presentation itself is the work: textiles and ceremony enacted Fijian protocols of honor and reciprocity.

practice.stimulus: A mask from the Torres Strait is made from plates of turtle shell, combining a human face with a bird form above, and decorated with feathers and shells.
practice.stem: Masks like this were primarily used in

choices.text: funerary and initiation ceremonies involving performance
church services
trade fairs with Europeans
sporting competitions

practice.explanation: The Buk mask's composite imagery connects human and animal realms in ritual.

distractors.B: It predates and is distinct from Christian worship.

practice.stem: Which challenge do works like malagan carvings, tapa, and the 1953 Fijian presentation pose to traditional museum display?

choices.text: Their meanings depend on performance, exchange, and impermanence, which a static display can't fully convey.
They are too small to see.
They were all made for museums originally.
They are copies of European works.

practice.explanation: Ceremony and relationship are central; museums preserve objects but often lose the actions that gave them meaning.

distractors.C: Most were made for ceremony or exchange.

practice.stimulus: Several Hawaiian feather capes were given to Captain James Cook and his crew in 1778–1779 and are now in European museums.
practice.stem: From a Hawaiian perspective, presenting these capes was most likely

choices.text: a high-status diplomatic act establishing relationships with powerful visitors
a sale of surplus goods
a sign that the capes had lost their value
a punishment

practice.explanation: Giving objects charged with mana honored visitors and created reciprocal obligations, a meaning lost when they became museum specimens.

distractors.C: The capes were among the most valuable objects Hawaiians made.

practice.stimulus: A wooden figure from the Micronesian atoll of Nukuoro is smooth and highly simplified, with an egg-shaped head lacking facial features.
practice.stem: Which statement best describes how such figures have been interpreted in different contexts?

choices.text: Locally they represented deities and were used in ritual; in Europe, modernists admired their abstraction as aesthetic form.
They were made in imitation of European modernist sculpture.
They were portraits of European explorers.
They were toys for children.

practice.explanation: The female deity from Nukuoro's simplicity was religious in origin but read as formalist abstraction by Western artists.

practice.stimulus: A large piece of Niuean bark cloth (hiapo) from around 1850–1900 is decorated with fine freehand geometric designs and, in some examples, small naturalistic figures influenced by contact with missionaries and traders.

choices.text: both continuity in Indigenous bark cloth traditions and change through new outside influences
a complete break with earlier traditions
industrial textile production
an imitation of Chinese porcelain

practice.explanation: The medium and making stayed traditional while some imagery responded to contact.

practice.stimulus: The work is a malagan display and mask, New Ireland Province, Papua New Guinea, c. twentieth century, wood, pigment, fiber, and shell.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe the purpose of malagan ceremonies.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain what typically happens to malagan objects after the ceremonies and why.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Describe one visual characteristic of malagan carvings and how it relates to their function.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Explain how museum collection of malagan objects relates to their intended life cycle.

rubric.description: Commemorating and honoring the dead, settling obligations, and marking the end of mourning.
Objects are destroyed, left to decay, or sold (often to outsiders).
Once the ceremony is complete, the objects have fulfilled their purpose; their value lay in the event and in the right to make them, not in preservation.
E.g., intricate openwork carving and bright painted patterns create visual drama during brief display; or layered imagery of ancestors and animals connects the dead to clan identity.

Sale to collectors after use was a permitted end for many objects, so museum holdings partly reflect local practice, but display preserves what was meant to be temporary and separates it from ceremony.

practice.sampleResponse:
(a) Malagan ceremonies honor and commemorate the dead, complete the process of mourning, and reaffirm clan relationships and obligations through feasts and exchange.

(b) After the ceremonies, malagan carvings are usually destroyed, left to decay, or sold. This is because their purpose was to be seen during the ceremony; once the dead have been honored, the objects are spent. What endures is the right to make a malagan design, not the object itself.

(c) Malagan carvings are often intricate openwork structures painted in bright red, black, white, and yellow. These dramatic forms are designed to impress the community during a brief, spectacular unveiling.

(d) Because selling used malagan objects was an accepted outcome, many museum examples left New Ireland legitimately after ceremonies. Yet museum display preserves something meant to be temporary, presenting it as permanent art rather than as the finished remains of a completed ritual.
